newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Peace key to revival of Angola's coffee sector.
newsitem.headline: Peace key to revival of Angola's coffee sector.

text.p: Angola hopes to breathe life into its once booming coffee sector, but the industry's revival is still overshadowed by the rigid borders between government and former rebel UNITA controlled areas.

UNITA controls 70 percent of some of the best coffee growing areas in the north and agricultural-rich central plateau regions and exports its coffee harvest via neighbouring Zaire. However, statistics for its exports are unavailable.

Secretary of State for Coffee, Gilberto Lutucutu, said early estimates showed the 1996 coffee crop in government areas would more than double to 5,000 tonnes of robusta for export. But this is just a drop in the ocean compared to the full potential.

"We foresee the harvest this year will be 5,000 tonnes. Depending on progress in peace we think we could eventually achieve 120,000 tonnes by 1998/99 with access to 240,000 hectares (600,000 acres)," Lutucutu told Reuters.
Angola's production last season was 2,000 tonnes.
The government and UNITA signed a peace pact in 1994 to end two decades of civil war and the successful implementation of the pact is key to the rebuilding of the coffee sector.
The peace plan foresees the dismantling of military posts on both sides and opening of all main roads throughout the country which will allow coffee producers access to markets.
The government currently produces robusta coffee in the provinces of Kwanza Norte, Kwanza Sul, Bengo, Uige and Benguela, as well as the northern enclave of Cabinda.

Angola was once one of the world's leading producers of coffee. In 1974 it ranked third globally producing 223,000 tonnes, but after independence from Portugal a year later production came to a standstill with the outbreak of civil war.
Many of the coffee plantations, formerly owned by the Portuguese, were abandoned and destroyed during the war. Others have stood untouched due to lack of financial resources and insecurity.
Angola liberalised its coffee sector in 1991/92 but the state coffee secretariate defines policy and quantity control through the National Coffee Institute (INCA).
Lutucutu said Angola's coffee industry needed $240 million over the next two years to boost production and a plan to overhaul the sector had been submitted to the International Coffee Organisation.
He said coffee was currently produced by a few private companies on plantations of up to 1,200 hectares each, and small family run operations of about one hectare.
Technical support teams have been put in place in government areas to assist producers, he said.
"Production is still very low per hectare. Families are producing about 250 kg (550 lbs) per hectare," Lutucutu said, adding that potential production per hectare was around 1,000 kg.
Foreign investors from Germany, the United States, Italy, South Africa and Portugal had shown interest in producing coffee in Angola, he said.
"Normally investors want large areas and currently we can't give this to them because much of the coffee areas are still controlled by UNITA," he said.

Lutucutu said Angola had the potential to rejoin the ranks of the world's top coffee exporters if peace held, financing was made available and producers and traders were able to safely transport their products.
"If this can happen, then Angola will be able to achieve maximum production within five to six years," he predicted.
